problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-3+z &=0 \\ 5y-1+3x &=2z+1 \\ 3z+2x-1 &=2y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find  $x+y+z.$
solution:
First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+z &=3 \\ 3x+5y-2z &=2 \\ 2x-2y+3z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix}-0+\begin{vmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(15-4)+(-6-10) \\  & =22-16 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

 

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 3 & 5\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}11 & 13 & -16 \\ 2 & 4 & -4 \\ -5 & -7 & 10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}11 & -13 & -16 \\ -2 & 4 & 4 \\ -5 & 7 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}24 \\ -24 \\ -30\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -4 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $x+y+z=4-4-5=-5.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2y+3z+x &=-1 \\ 4z+y &=1 \\ 5x+6y-3 &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$
solution:
We organize the system so that it’s in the correct order first:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y+3z &=-1 \\ y+4z &=1 \\ 5x+6y &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 5 & 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 5 & 6 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 5 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-24)-2(-20)+3(-5) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 5 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 5 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 5 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-24 & -20 & -5 \\ -18 & -15 & -4 \\ 5 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 20 & -5 \\ 18 & -15 & 4 \\ 5 & -4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 18 & 5 \\ 20 & -15 & -4 \\ -5 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 18 & 5 \\ 20 & -15 & -4 \\ -5 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 18 & 5 \\ 20 & -15 & -4 \\ -5 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}42 \\ -35 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=42,y=-35,z=9.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}z+2y+7x &=1 \\ 3y-z &=-2 \\ 4y-2z-3x &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$
solution:
We organize the system so that it’s in the correct order first:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}7x+2y+z &=1 \\ 3y-z &=-2 \\ -3x+4y-2z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}7 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ -3 & 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}7 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ -3 & 4 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =7\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 4 & -2\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ -3 & -2\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =7(-6+4)-2(-3)+1(9) \\  & =-14+6+9 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 4 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ -3 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 4 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}7 & 1 \\ -3 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}7 & 2 \\ -3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}7 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}7 & 2 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -3 & 9 \\ -8 & -11 & 34 \\ -5 & -7 & 21\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 9 \\ 8 & -11 & -34 \\ -5 & 7 & 21\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 8 & -5 \\ 3 & -11 & 7 \\ 9 & -34 & 21\text{ }\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 8 & -5 \\ 3 & -11 & 7 \\ 9 & -34 & 21\text{ }\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 8 & -5 \\ 3 & -11 & 7 \\ 9 & -34 & 21\text{ }\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-18 \\ 25 \\ 77\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=-18,\,y=25,\,z=77.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2y+3z &=-1-x \\ 4y &=-5z \\ x+6z-3 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$
solution:
We organize the system so that it’s in the correct order first:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y+3z &=-1 \\ 4y+5z &=0 \\ x+6z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}4 & 5 \\ 0 & 6\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}0 & 5 \\ 1 & 6\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(24)-2(-5)+3(0-4) \\  & =24+10-12 \\  & =22.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}4 & 5 \\ 0 & 6\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 5 \\ 1 & 6\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 6\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 5\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}24 & -5 & -4 \\ 12 & 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 5 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}24 & 5 & -4 \\ -12 & 3 & 2 \\ -2 & -5 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}24 & -12 & -2 \\ 5 & 3 & -5 \\ -4 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{22}\begin{bmatrix}24 & -12 & -2 \\ 5 & 3 & -5 \\ -4 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{22}\begin{bmatrix}24 & -12 & -2 \\ 5 & 3 & -5 \\ -4 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{22}\begin{bmatrix}-30 \\ -20 \\ 16\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{15}{11} \\ -\frac{10}{11} \\ \frac{8}{11}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=-\frac{15}{11},y=-\frac{10}{11},z=\frac{8}{11}.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3z-y+x-5 &=0 \\ y+2x+2z &=1 \\ z-2x-2y &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$
solution:
We organize the system so that it’s in the correct order first:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+3z &=5 \\ 2x+y+2z &=1 \\ -2x-2y+z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix}-(-1)\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(1+4)+1(2+4)+3(-4+2) \\  & =5+6-6 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & 7 & -4 \\ -5 & -4 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}5 & -6 & -2 \\ -5 & 7 & 4 \\ -5 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & -5 & -5 \\ -6 & 7 & 4 \\ -2 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -5 & -5 \\ -6 & 7 & 4 \\ -2 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -5 & -5 \\ -6 & 7 & 4 \\ -2 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -\frac{19}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=3,y=-\frac{19}{5},z=-\frac{3}{5}.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x-2y+3z &=0 \\ 8x-3y+5z &=9 \\ 7x-2y+4z &=-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$
solution:
We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 & 3 \\ 8 & -3 & 5 \\ 7 & -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 9 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}4 & -2 & 3 \\ 8 & -3 & 5 \\ 7 & -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 5 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix}-(-2)\begin{vmatrix}8 & 5 \\ 7 & 4\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}8 & -3 \\ 7 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4(-12+10)+2(32-35)+3(-16+21) \\  & =-8-6+15 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 5 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}8 & 5 \\ 7 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}8 & -3 \\ 7 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 7 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 7 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 5\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 8 & 5\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}4 & -2 \\ 8 & -3\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -3 & 5 \\ -2 & -5 & 6 \\ -1 & -4 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 5 \\ 2 & -5 & -6 \\ -1 & 4 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -5 & 4 \\ 5 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -5 & 4 \\ 5 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -5 & 4 \\ 5 & -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 9 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}19 \\ -49 \\ -58\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=19,y=-49,z=-58.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+3y+z &=6 \\ 4x+7y+2z &=0 \\ 3x+y+z &=1\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$
solution:
We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 7 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 7 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}7 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}4 & 7 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(7-2)-3(-2)+1(4-21) \\  & =10+6-17 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}7 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}4 & 7 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 7 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 4 & 7\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & -2 & -17 \\ 2 & -1 & -7 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 2 & -17 \\ -2 & -1 & 7 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & -2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -17 & 7 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -17 & 7 & 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 17 & -7 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 17 & -7 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-29 \\ -12 \\ 100\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=-29,y=-12,z=100.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-z &=0 \\ x+y+3z &=2 \\ 3x-2y+z &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$
solution:
We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix}-0\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(1-3(-2))+0-1(-2-3) \\  & =1+6+2+3 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & -8 & -5 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}7 & 8 & -5 \\ 2 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}7 & 2 & 1 \\ 8 & 4 & -4 \\ -5 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 2 & 1 \\ 8 & 4 & -4 \\ -5 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 2 & 1 \\ 8 & 4 & -4 \\ -5 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ -8 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=\frac{2}{3},y=-\frac{2}{3},z=\frac{2}{3}.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2y+2z &=1 \\ x+y+z &=3 \\ y+2z &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$
solution:
We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-2(2)+2(1) \\  & =-4+2 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 8 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{2} \\ 4 \\ -\frac{7}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=\frac{5}{2},y=4,z=-\frac{7}{2}.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+z &=1 \\ 2x-2z &=2+2y \\ 2y+4z &=2x-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find  $x+y+z.$
solution:
First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+z &=1 \\ 2x-2y-2z &=2 \\ -2x+2y+4z &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-(8-4)+(4-4) \\  & =-4+0 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -4 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{-4}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x+y+z=2+1+0=3.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+z+x &=2 \\ -3z+y &=3 \\ 2x+y &=4-4z\end{aligned}\right.
$$
solution:
We organize the system so that it’s in the correct order first:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=2 \\ y-3z &=3 \\ 2x+y+4z &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 2 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 2 & 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4+3)-(0+6)+(0-2) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 6 & -2 \\ 3 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}7 & -6 & -2 \\ -3 & 2 & 1 \\ -4 & 3 & 1\text{ }\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}7 & -3 & -4 \\ -6 & 2 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -3 & -4 \\ -6 & 2 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 3 & 4 \\ 6 & -2 & -3 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 3 & 4 \\ 6 & -2 & -3 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=11,y=-6,z=-3.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}z+x &=2 \\ 2y-3z &=1 \\ 2z-y &=-3x+3\end{aligned}\right.
$$
solution:
We organize the system so that it’s in the correct order first:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+z &=2 \\ 2y-3z &=1 \\ 3x-y+2z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}-0\begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4-3)-0+(0-6) \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 9 & -6 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -9 & -6 \\ -1 & -1 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -9 & -1 & 3 \\ -6 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -9 & -1 & 3 \\ -6 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -9 & -1 & 3 \\ -6 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=1,y=2,z=1.$

problem:
Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+z &=4x+y+2 \\ x+y &=2z+2 \\ y &=x-y+z+1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find the solution $x=[x,y,z]^{T}$ of the system by computing the inverse of the coefficient matrix.

|  |  | {{field-1}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x=\,\,$ |  | {{field-2}} |  |
|  |  | {{field-3}} |  |
solution:
First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3x-y+z &=2 \\ x+y-2z &=2 \\ -x+2y-z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-3\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix}-(-1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-3(-1+4)+(-1-2)+(2+1) \\  & =-9-3+3 \\  & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -3 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 & -7 \\ 1 & 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 7 \\ 1 & -5 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & -5 \\ 3 & 7 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & -5 \\ 3 & 7 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & -5 \\ 3 & 7 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 9 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+2z &=0 \\ x+2y+3z &=2 \\ 3x+y+z &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$
solution:
We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-1(1-9)+2(1-6) \\  & =+8-10 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -8 & -5 \\ -1 & -6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 8 & -5 \\ 1 & -6 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{2} \\ 9 \\ -\frac{9}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=-\frac{5}{2},y=9,z=-\frac{9}{2}.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y-2z &=-1 \\ 3x-z &=5+3y \\ 3z-2y &=6-x\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find  $x+y+z.$
solution:
First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y-2z &=-1 \\ 3x-3y-z &=5 \\ x-2y+3z &=6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}+(-2)\begin{vmatrix}3 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(-9-2)-(9+1)-2(-6+3) \\  & =-22-10+6 \\  & =-26.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -3 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -3\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 10 & -3 \\ -1 & 8 & -5 \\ -7 & 4 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-11 & -10 & -3 \\ 1 & 8 & 5 \\ -7 & -4 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 1 & -7 \\ -10 & 8 & -4 \\ -3 & 5 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{26}\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 1 & -7 \\ -10 & 8 & -4 \\ -3 & 5 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =-\frac{1}{26}\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 1 & -7 \\ -10 & 8 & -4 \\ -3 & 5 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{26}\begin{bmatrix}-26 \\ 26 \\ -26\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x+y+z=1-1+1=1.$

problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations using matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}3y+x+z &=0 \\ z+4y-5 &=2 \\ 1+2x-y &=-3\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$
solution:
First, we organize the system so that the variables are in the correct order and every variable has a coefficient:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}x+3y+z &=0 \\ 0x+4y+z &=7 \\ 2x-y+0z &=-4\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

![](images/e8/e816a0fcde823bc6f6e88dff0a02c1877275cbed75757c1eb366fb224629127e.svg)

Now, the solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is given by $\mathbf{x}= A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$ So, we compute $A^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1*: Find the determinant of $A.$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & =1\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1)-3(-2)+(-8) \\  & =1+6-8 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2*: Compute the matrix of minors.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 4 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & -7 \\ -1 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3*:  Find the matrix of cofactors.

![](images/be/beb80ea3185fc723c294313b63274554ec8af3531ed5643173a6127c59a21bb3.svg)

*Step 4*: Transpose the matrix of cofactors.

![](images/e6/e6fac5dd0a9918a03ce7c14e9cd05a06c6d11e95346f261ec75d6ebea09de1d6.svg)

*Step 5*: Apply the inverse matrix formula.

![](images/72/72b9d627d372d7a64a271b555b0d4cbb89b2bf9d602cdec64b1d8987a5e21521.svg)

Finally, we can calculate the solution as follows:

$$

problem:
$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $v$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $v$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A$
- **II.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A$
- **III.** $v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $1$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
solution:
A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{2}$ of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{1}\ne 0.$ Recall that an *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$ 

With this in mind, let's examine our statements.

First, we compute $A-3I:$

$$
A-3I=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

- Next, we find the image of $v$ under the action of $A-3I:$

$$
(A-3I)v=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}={{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{w}\ne 0
$$

- Since we got a nonzero vector in the last step, we now compute the image of $w$ under the action of $A-3I:$

$$
(A-3I)w=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=0
$$

So, we obtain the following chain of maps:

$$
{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{A-3I\,}{\to }{{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{0}
$$

Here, we see that $A-3I$ maps $v$ to $0$ in $2$ steps.

Therefore:

$\,$ *$v$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of $A.$*

So, the correct answer is "II only."

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 3 & 7 \\ 3 & -2 & 4\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form.
solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form using the standard algorithm for Gaussian elimination, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 3 & 7 \\ 3 & -2 & 4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{7}{2} \\ 3 & -2 & 4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{7}{2} \\ 0 & -\frac{13}{2} & -\frac{13}{2}\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{2}{13}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{7}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 1 & 8 \\ -1 & -2 & 3\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system represented by the matrix.
solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 1 & 8 \\ -1 & -2 & 3\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+1\cdot {R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & -1 & 11\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-1\cdot {R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & -11\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y &=8 \\ y &=-11,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-11$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(-11)=8\,⇒\,x=8+11=19.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=19$ and $y=-11.$

problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 7 & -2 \\ 2 & 10 & 0\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system represented by the matrix.
solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 7 & -2 \\ 2 & 10 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 7 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 7 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+7y &=-2 \\ y &=-1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-1$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x+7(-1)=-2\,⇒\,x=-2+7=5.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=5$ and $y=-1.$

problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}3 & -6 & 10 \\ 2 & -3 & 5\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system represented by the matrix.
solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}3 & -6 & 10 \\ 2 & -3 & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & \frac{10}{3} \\ 2 & -3 & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & \frac{10}{3} \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{5}{3}\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=\frac{10}{3} \\ y &=-\frac{5}{3},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-\frac{5}{3}$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x-2(-\frac{5}{3})=\frac{10}{3}\,⇒\,x=\frac{10}{3}-\frac{10}{3}=0.
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=0$ and $y=-\frac{5}{3}.$

problem:

$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system represented by the matrix.
solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & -6 & -9 \\ 1 & -2 & -4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & -\frac{9}{2} \\ 1 & -2 & -4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & -\frac{9}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-3y &=-\frac{9}{2} \\ y &=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=\frac{1}{2}$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x-3(\frac{1}{2})=-\frac{9}{2}\,⇒\,x=-\frac{9}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=-3.
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=-3$ and $y=\frac{1}{2}.$

$$

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & -8 \\ 2 & 4 & 4\end{array}\right].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & -8 \\ 2 & 4 & 4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & -8 \\ 0 & 10 & 20\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{10}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-3y &=-8 \\ y &=2,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=2$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x-3(2)=-8\,⇒\,x=-2.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-2$ and $y=2.$

problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+\frac{1}{3}y &=11 \\ 3x+\frac{1}{5}y &=9.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{3} & 11 \\ 3 & \frac{1}{5} & 9\end{array}\right].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{3} & 11 \\ 3 & \frac{1}{5} & 9\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{3} & 11 \\ 0 & -\frac{4}{5} & -24\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{5}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{3} & 11 \\ 0 & 1 & 30\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+\frac{1}{3}y &=11 \\ y &=30,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=30$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x+\frac{1}{3}(30)=11\,⇒\,x=11-10=1.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=1$ and $y=30.$

problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-4y &=6 \\ 4x-7y &=10.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & -4 & 6 \\ 4 & -7 & 10\end{array}\right].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & -4 & 6 \\ 4 & -7 & 10\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & -7 & 10\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=3 \\ y &=-2,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-2$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x-2(-2)=3\,⇒\,x=-1.
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=-1$ and $y=-2.$

problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-x+5y &=5 \\ x-6y &=5.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=
	\left[
	\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 5 & 5 \\ 1 & -6 & 5\end{array}
	\right].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 5 & 5 \\ 1 & -6 & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -5 & -5 \\ 1 & -6 & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -5 & -5 \\ 0 & -1 & 10\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -5 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & -10\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-5y &=-5 \\ y &=-10,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-10$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x-5(-10)=-5 
	\quad\Rightarrow\quad
	x=-55.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-55$ and $y=-10.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -55,-10 \rangle.$

problem: Find an equation of the plane that contains the point $P(2,-5,3)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n=⟨-1,2,-3⟩.$
solution:
First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨2,-5,3⟩,$ and $n=⟨-1,2,-3⟩$ is normal to the plane.

The equation of the plane that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is perpendicular to the vector $n$ can be given as

$$
(r-p)\cdot n=0,
$$

where $r$ is the position vector of any point on the plane, and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-1,2,-3⟩ & =⟨2,-5,3⟩\cdot ⟨-1,2,-3⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-1,2,-3⟩ & =-21.\end{aligned}
$$

problem: A nonzero vector $⟨a,\,b,\,0⟩$ is parallel to the plane $r\cdot ⟨6,-2,0⟩=-14.$ What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
solution:
We need a vector $v=⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩$ that is parallel to the given plane. 

From the equation $r\cdot ⟨6,-2,0⟩=-14$ of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨6,-2,0⟩.$ So, $v⊥n$ and we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨6,-2,0⟩ & =0 \\ 6{t}_{1}-2{t}_{2} & =0 \\ {t}_{2} & =3{t}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain 

$$
v=⟨{t}_{1},3{t}_{1},{t}_{3}⟩,
$$

where ${t}_{1},{t}_{3}\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

We are told that the third component of $v$ eqauls $0.$ So, we must set ${t}_{3}=0.$ 

Since $v$ is nonzero, we can pick any ${t}_{1}\ne 0.$ For example, setting ${t}_{1}=1$, we get

$$
v=⟨1,\,3,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{3}.$

$$
\mathbf{v}=\langle t_1, 2t_1 + 4t_3, t_3 \rangle,

$$
\mathbf{v} = \langle 0,\, \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{4}, \, \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{1} \rangle.
$$

Therefore, $\dfrac{b}{c} = 4.$

problem:
Find an equation of the plane that passes through the point $Q(2,-3,5)$ and is perpendicular to the line that goes through the points 
$A(3,2,-8)$ and $B(1,2,-5).$
solution:
First, we note that the position vector of $Q$ is $q=⟨2,-3,5⟩.$

Since the line  passes through the points $A(3,2,-8)$ and $B(1,2,-5)$, we can find a vector that is parallel to the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨1,2,-5⟩-⟨3,2,-8⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,0,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, a normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨-2,0,3⟩.$

Therefore, the equation of the plane is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-q)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-q\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =q\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-2,0,3⟩ & =⟨2,-3,5⟩\cdot ⟨-2,0,3⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-2,0,3⟩ & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Find an equation of the plane that passes through the point $Q(-2,2,0)$ and is perpendicular to the line 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=3-4t \\ y &=1+6t \\ z &=-1+2t.\end{aligned}\right.
$$
solution:
Note that the position vector of $Q$ is $q=⟨-2,2,0⟩.$ Converting the parametric equations of the line to vector form, we get

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=3-4t \\ y &=1+6t \\ z &=-1+2t\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,⟨x,y,z⟩=⟨3,1,-1⟩+t\text{ }{{⟨-4,6,2⟩}_{⏟}}_{v}.
$$

 

The direction vector of the line is $v=⟨-4,6,2⟩,$ so a normal vector to the plane is 

$$
n=v=⟨-4,6,2⟩.
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-q)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-q\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =q\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-4,6,2⟩ & =⟨-2,2,0⟩\cdot ⟨-4,6,2⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-4,6,2⟩ & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

problem:

$$

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in terms of the components of $x=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}?$
solution:
**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =1{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(-2){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(-2){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={x}_{1}({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(-2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Since the matrix of the quadratic form must be symmetric, we rewrite our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =1{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\  & +\,4{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must split the coefficient of $8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ between the entries 

$$

$$

of our matrix. So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, $a=1$ and $b=4.$ Finally, 

$$
a+b=1+4=5.
$$

problem:
Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** Any $3\times 2$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
- **II.** The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ -1 & -5\end{bmatrix}$ has one negative singular value.
- **III.** Any $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

Select all that apply.
solution:

problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}?$
solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}2-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 8-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ 16-2\lambda -8\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -10) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =10,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{10} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=0\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-1) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}?$
solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}9-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 9-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(9-\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$

problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}?$
solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}5-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 8-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda -5\lambda +40-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda +36 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(3,1,-1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,1,3⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=\sqrt{14}.$
solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨3,1,-1⟩+t⟨2,1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨3,1,-1⟩+t⟨2,1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨3,1,-1⟩+t⟨2,1,3⟩)-⟨3,1,-1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨2,1,3⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,t,\,3t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{14},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{14} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{14} \\ |⟨2t,\,t,\,3t⟩| & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}+(3t)^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{14{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \pm t\sqrt{14} & =\sqrt{14} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨3,1,-1⟩+1⟨2,1,3⟩=⟨5,2,2⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨3,1,-1⟩-1⟨2,1,3⟩=⟨1,0,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(5,2,2)$ and ${A}_{2}(1,0,-4).$

$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{5},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{5} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{5} \\ |⟨-t,\,0,\,2t⟩| & =\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{(-t)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} & =\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+0+4{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{5} \\ \pm \sqrt{5}t & =\sqrt{5} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}

In our case, $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S} & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{(\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =(14)^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{14}\begin{bmatrix}9 & -6 & 3 \\ -6 & 4 & -2 \\ 3 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

solution:
First, we find the orthogonal projection matrix onto ${S}^{⊥}=\text{Span}{a}.$

Using the formula for the orthogonal projection matrix

$$
{P}_{{S}^{⊥}}=a({a}^{T}\,a)^{-1}{a}^{T},
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}{(\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={9}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 & -4 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ -4 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

First, we find the orthogonal projection matrix onto $S^\perp = \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.$

$$
P_{S^\perp} = \mathbf{a} (\mathbf{a}^T\!\mathbf{a})^{-1} \mathbf{a}^T,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={6}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

U=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}5\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,V=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{bmatrix},\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{50}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{50}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{50}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -3 \\ -4 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{2}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {5}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
The standard matrix $T$ of a linear transformation $T$ and the vector $b\in {R}^{3}$ are given below. Determine if there exists a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ such that $T(x)=b.$
In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2},$ where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -5 & 3 \\ 4 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ -7 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}
$$
solution:
Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, we find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b],$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -5 & 3 & 9 \\ 4 & -1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & -3\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -5 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & -11 & 11 & 11 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & -3\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{3}{11}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -5 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & -11 & 11 & 11 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Hence, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. 
Now, from the second equation, we get 

$$
-11{x}_{2}+11{x}_{3}=11\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-1+{x}_{3}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation gives 

$$
-2{x}_{1}-5(-1+{x}_{3})+3{x}_{3}=9\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-2-{x}_{3}.
$$

As a result, the general solution is given by 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2-{x}_{3} \\ -1+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
x=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $T(x)=b.$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-2-1=-3.$

solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 & -3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & -1 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

problem:

$$
solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & 1 & -6 \\ 3 & 5 & -16 & 10 \\ -1 & -1 & 5 & -3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b]$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 & 3 & 4 \\ -2 & 4 & 1 & -6 & -5 \\ 3 & 5 & -16 & 10 & 4 \\ -1 & -1 & 5 & -3 & 5\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 8 & -10 & 1 & -8 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 & 0 & 9\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-4{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1 & -20 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 12\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

From the fourth equation, we get the false statement $0=12.$ Therefore, the system is inconsistent, and we conclude that  $b\notin \text{Im}(T).$

problem:

solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -2 & 2 \\ -1 & 4 & -5 & -2 \\ 3 & 7 & -4 & 6\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{2}{7}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Hence, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.
Now, from the second equation, we get 

$$
7{x}_{2}-7{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation gives 

$$
{x}_{1}+3({x}_{3})-2{x}_{3}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2-{x}_{3}.
$$

As a result, the general solution is given by 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=1$, we have

$$
x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $T(x)=b.$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=1+1=2.$

problem: Let $T:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}-2x+y \\ -x+4y \\ -3x-5y\end{bmatrix}$ be a linear transformation. Determine the value of $k$ for which the vector $v=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -4 \\ k\end{bmatrix}$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T).$
solution:
The vector $v$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T)$ if there exists a vector $u=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}$ such that $T(u)=v.$ 

Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-2x+y \\ -x+4y \\ -3x-5y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -4 \\ k\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2x+y &=6 \\ -x+4y &=-4 \\ -3x-5y &=k.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=4+4y$, which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+y & =6 \\ -2(4+4y)+y & =6 \\ -7y & =14 \\ y & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4+4y \\  & =4+4(-2) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x=-4$ and $y=-2$ into the third equation and obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x-5y & =k \\ -3(-4)-5(-2) & =k \\ k & =22.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $v\in \text{Im}(T)$ when $k=22.$

problem: Let $T=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -8 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0 \\ -2 & 10 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ be the standard matrix of the linear transformation $T.$ Determine the value of $k$ for which the vector $v=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 8 \\ k\end{bmatrix}$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T).$
solution:
The vector $v$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T)$ if there exists a vector $u=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}$ such that $T(u)=v.$

Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}T\cdot u & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}3 & -8 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0 \\ -2 & 10 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 8 \\ k\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3x-8y \\ 2x-4y \\ -2x+10y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 8 \\ k\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x-8y &=6 \\ 2x-4y &=8 \\ -2x+10y &=k.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=4+2y$, which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-8y & =6 \\ 3(4+2y)-8y & =6 \\ -2y & =-6 \\ y & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4+2y \\  & =4+2(3) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x=10$ and $y=3$ into the third equation and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+10y & =k \\ -2(10)+10(3) & =k \\ k & =10.\end{aligned}

problem: Let $T=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ be the standard matrix of the linear transformation $T.$ Determine the value of $k$ for which the vector $v=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 7 \\ k\end{bmatrix}$  belongs to $\text{Im}(T).$
solution:
The vector $v$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T)$ if there exists a vector $u=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}$ such that $T(u)=v.$

Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}T\cdot u & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 7 \\ k\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2x-4y \\ x-3y \\ -x+4y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 7 \\ k\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-4y &=2 \\ x-3y &=7 \\ -x+4y &=k.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=7+3y$, which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-4y & =2 \\ 2(7+3y)-4y & =2 \\ 2y & =-12 \\ y & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7+3y \\  & =7+3(-6) \\  & =-11.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x=-11$ and $y=-6$ into the third equation and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+4y & =k \\ -(-11)+4(-6) & =k \\ k & =-13.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $v\in \text{Im}(T)$ when $k=-13.$

problem: Let $T:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}3x+y \\ x+2y \\ -2x+7y\end{bmatrix}$ be a linear transformation. Determine the value of $k$ for which the vector $v=\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 8 \\ k\end{bmatrix}$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T).$
solution:
The vector $v$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T)$ if there exists a vector $u=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}$ such that $T(u)=v.$ 

Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3x+y \\ x+2y \\ -2x+7y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 8 \\ k\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+y &=9 \\ x+2y &=8 \\ -2x+7y &=k.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=8-2y$, which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+y & =9 \\ 3(8-2y)+y & =9 \\ -5y & =-15 \\ y & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =8-2y \\  & =8-2(3) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x=2$ and $y=3$ into the third equation and obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+7y & =k \\ -2(2)+7(3) & =k \\ k & =17.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $v\in \text{Im}(T)$ when $k=17.$

problem: Let $T=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -5 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ be the standard matrix of the linear transformation $T.$ Determine the value of $k$ for which the vector $v=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ k \\ -1\end{bmatrix}$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T).$
solution:
The vector $v$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T)$ if there exists a vector $u=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}$ such that $T(u)=v.$

$$

$$

This gives the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3x+2y &=5 \\ -2y &=k \\ -5x+y &=-1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get $y=5x-1$, which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+2y & =5 \\ -3x+2(5x-1) & =5 \\ 7x & =7 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5x-1 \\  & =5(1)-1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=4$ into the second equation and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-2y & =k \\ -2(4) & =k \\ k & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $v\in \text{Im}(T)$ when $k=-8.$

problem:
Calculate ${B}^{-1}$, where 
$B=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$
solution:
Given a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix},
$$

the inverse of $B$ can be found using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(B)}\begin{bmatrix}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we compute the determinant:

$$
det(B)=2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1=-1
$$

Using the formula, then, the inverse is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(B)}\begin{bmatrix}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can verify the result as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B{B}^{-1} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓ \\ {B}^{-1}B & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

the inverse of $A$ can be found using the following formula: $$ \begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}\begin{bmatrix}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ First, we compute the determinant: $$ \det(A) = 1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot (-2) = 1 $$ Using the formula, then, the inverse is given by $$ \begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}\begin{bmatrix}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{bmatrix}. \\ & =\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -0 \\ -(-2) & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ We can verify the result as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}A{A}^{-1} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & ={I}_{2}\,✓ \\ {A}^{-1}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned} $$

problem: If $A = \begin{bmatrix}k & 2 \\ 2 & k\end{bmatrix}$ is a singular matrix, calculate the value(s) of $k$.
If $A=\begin{bmatrix}k & k \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ is a singular matrix, calculate the value of $k.$
solution:
The matrix $A$ is singular if and only if $det(A)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =k\cdot 1-k\cdot 2 \\  & =k-2k \\  & =-k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-k & =0 \\ k & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $k$ is $k=0.$

problem: If $F=\begin{bmatrix}3 & t \\ t & 3\end{bmatrix}$ is a singular matrix, calculate the value(s) of $t.$
solution:
The matrix $F$ is singular if and only if $det(F)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(F) & =3\cdot 3-t\cdot t \\  & =9-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9-{t}^{2} & =0 \\ {t}^{2} & =9 \\ t & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the values of $t$ are $t=\pm 3.$

problem:
Let $B=\begin{bmatrix}2x+4 & 0 \\ 15 & -x-3\end{bmatrix}$
be a singular matrix. **In ascending order**, the values of $x$ are

$x=$
{{field-1}}$\,$ and $\,x=$
{{field-2}}.
solution:
The matrix $B$ is singular if and only if $det(B)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =(2x+4)\cdot (-x-3)-0\cdot 15 \\  & =-2{x}^{2}-6x-4x-12 \\  & =-2{x}^{2}-10x-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}^{2}-10x-12 & =0 \\ -2({x}^{2}+5x+6) & =0 \\ (x+3)(x+2) & =0 \\ x & =-3,-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the values of $x$ are

$$
x=-3\,\text{and}\,x=-2.
$$

problem:
Let $B=\begin{bmatrix}2x+1 & x-40 \\ 1 & -x\end{bmatrix}$
be a singular matrix. **In ascending order**, the values of $x$ are

$x=$
{{field-1}}$\,$ and $\,x=$
{{field-2}}.
solution:
The matrix $B$ is singular if and only if $det(B)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =(2x+1)\cdot (-x)-(x-40)\cdot 1 \\  & =-2{x}^{2}-x-x+40 \\  & =-2{x}^{2}-2x+40.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}^{2}-2x+40 & =0 \\ -2({x}^{2}+x-20) & =0 \\ -2(x-4)(x+5) & =0 \\ x & =4,-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the values of $x$ are

$$
x=-5\,\text{and}\,x=4.
$$

problem:

be a singular matrix. **In ascending order**, the values of $x$ are

$x=$
{{field-1}}$\,$ and $\,x=$
{{field-2}}.
solution:
The matrix $B$ is singular if and only if $det(B)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =3\cdot 0-(-x+7)\cdot (x-5) \\  & ={x}^{2}-5x-7x+35 \\  & ={x}^{2}-12x+35.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $x:$

problem: If $V=\begin{bmatrix}7 & y \\ 5 & y\end{bmatrix}$ is a singular matrix, calculate the value of $y.$
solution:
The matrix $V$ is singular if and only if $det(V)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(V) & =7\cdot y-5\cdot y \\  & =7y-5y \\  & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $y$ is $y=0.$

problem: If $H=\begin{bmatrix}5 & c \\ c & 5\end{bmatrix}$ is a singular matrix, calculate the value(s) of $c.$
solution:
The matrix $H$ is singular if and only if $det(H)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(H) & =5\cdot 5-c\cdot c \\  & =25-{c}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $c:$

$$
\begin{aligned}25-{c}^{2} & =0 \\ {c}^{2} & =25 \\ c & =\pm 5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the values of $c$ are $c=\pm 5.$

problem: If $M=\begin{bmatrix}t & 4 \\ t & 10\end{bmatrix}$ is a singular matrix, calculate the value of $t.$
solution:
The matrix $M$ is singular if and only if $det(M)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =t\cdot 10-t\cdot 4 \\  & =10t-4t \\  & =6t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6t & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $t$ is $t=0.$

problem:

 \begin{bmatrix}1-k & 2 \\ 2 & 1-k\end{bmatrix}
$$
 is a singular matrix, calculate the value(s) of $k.$
solution:
The matrix $A$ is singular if and only if $\det(A)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =(1-k)(1-k)-4 \\  & ={k}^{2}-2k-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
